Ch1: 함정 구간 전수 보존 — 12명 이름(Reuben·Simeon·Levi·Judah·Issachar·Zebulun·Benjamin·Dan·Naphtali·Gad·Asher), 70명, 저장 도시 Pithom·Rameses, 산파 Shiphrah·Puah, 벽돌·진흙·들판 노동, 나일강 명령
paragraphs: So here's the family roll call — the Israelites who moved to Egypt with Jacob, each bringing their whole crew: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Benjamin, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. Seventy people total, all Jacob's descendants. Joseph was already down in Egypt.
Then Joseph died, and his brothers too — that whole generation was gone. But the Israelites? They kept multiplying like crazy. Seriously, a total population explosion — they filled up the whole land.
§ A New King Who Never Knew Joseph

Then a brand-new king took over Egypt — and this guy had no idea who Joseph was. He freaked out and told his people, "These Israelites are getting way too many for us to handle. We need a plan to keep them under control. If there's a war, they might join our enemies — or just pack up and leave us!"

So they split the Israelites into work gangs and forced them into brutal labor under harsh foremen. They built Pharaoh's storage cities, Pithom and Rameses. But here's the wild part — the harder the Egyptians pushed them, the more the Israelites multiplied. Kids everywhere! The Egyptians started to seriously hate them and cracked down even harder, crushing them with slave labor. They made their lives miserable — forcing them to make bricks and mortar and do back-breaking work out in the fields. They just kept piling on the work, burying them under the brutal workload.

The king of Egypt called in the two Hebrew midwives — Shiphrah and Puah. He ordered them, "When you deliver Hebrew women's babies, check whether it's a boy or a girl. If it's a boy, kill him. If it's a girl, let her live."
But the midwives respected God way too much to obey the king — they let the baby boys live. The king dragged them back in and demanded, "Why didn't you follow my orders? You let those babies live!"
The midwives told Pharaoh, "Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women — they're tough and strong. By the time a midwife gets there, the baby's already born!"
God was pleased with the midwives. The Israelites kept growing into a strong, huge people. And because the midwives honored God, God blessed them with families of their own.
So Pharaoh gave a brutal order to all his people: "Every Hebrew boy that's born — throw him into the Nile. Let the girls live."
title: Oppressed in Egypt

paragraphs: § Moses

A guy from the tribe of Levi married a Levite woman. She got pregnant and had a baby boy. She could tell there was something special about him, so she hid him. She kept him hidden for three months. When she couldn't hide him anymore, she made a little basket-boat out of papyrus, sealed it up with tar and pitch to make it waterproof, and put the baby inside. Then she set it floating in the reeds at the edge of the Nile.

The baby's big sister stayed at a distance, watching to see what would happen. Then Pharaoh's daughter came down to the Nile to take a bath, with her servants strolling along the bank. She spotted the basket-boat floating in the reeds and sent one of her maids to grab it. She opened it — and there was the baby, crying! Her heart melted. She said, "This must be one of the Hebrew babies."
Then his sister stepped up: "Want me to go find a Hebrew woman to nurse the baby for you?"
Pharaoh's daughter said, "Yes, go!" So the girl ran and got the baby's own mother.
Pharaoh's daughter told her, "Take this baby and nurse him for me — I'll pay you." The woman took the child and nursed him.
Once the boy was weaned, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, who adopted him as her own son. She named him Moses — "Pulled-Out" — saying, "I pulled him out of the water."

Years went by and Moses grew up. One day he went out to see his fellow Israelites and watched them doing brutal slave labor. Then he saw an Egyptian beating up a Hebrew — one of his own people! He looked around; nobody was watching. So he killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand.
The next day he went back out and saw two Hebrew men fighting. He said to the one who started it, "Why are you hitting your neighbor?"
The guy snapped back, "Who do you think you are, bossing us around? You gonna kill me like you killed that Egyptian?" Moses panicked — "Uh oh. People know about this."
When Pharaoh heard about it, he tried to have Moses killed. But Moses ran for it and escaped to Midian. He sat down by a well.

The priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came to draw water, filling up the troughs to water their father's sheep. Some shepherds showed up and chased the girls off — but Moses jumped in to rescue them and helped them water their sheep.
When they got home to their dad Reuel, he said, "Wow, you're back early. How come?"
"Some Egyptian guy," they said, "rescued us from those shepherds. He even drew water for us and watered the sheep!"
He said, "Well, where is he? Why'd you leave him out there? Invite him in to eat with us!"

Moses decided to stay with the man, who gave him his daughter Zipporah — "Bird" — as his wife. She had a son, and Moses named him Gershom — "Sojourner" — saying, "I'm a stranger living in a foreign land."
A lot of years passed, and the king of Egypt died. But the Israelites were still groaning under slavery, crying out for help. Their cries rose all the way up to God.
God heard their groaning. God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God saw what was happening to Israel. God understood.
title: Moses Is Born

paragraphs: Moses was out shepherding the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the sheep to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. That's when the angel of God showed up — in flames of fire blazing out of the middle of a bush! Moses looked closer. The bush was on fire but it wasn't burning up.
Moses said, "Whoa, what's going on here? This is wild! Why isn't the bush burning up?"
God saw that Moses had stopped to check it out. God called to him from inside the bush, "Moses! Moses!" Moses answered, "Yes? I'm right here!"
God said, "Don't come any closer. Take off your sandals — you're standing on holy ground."
Then he said, "I am the God of your father — the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob." Moses covered his face, terrified to look at God.

God said, "I've been watching my people's suffering in Egypt for a long time. I've heard them crying out to escape their slave drivers — I know exactly how much pain they're in. So I've come down to rescue them, to rip them out of Egypt's grip and bring them out of that country to a good land with wide-open spaces — a land flowing with milk and honey. Right now it belongs to the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites."

"The Israelites' cry for help has reached me, and I've seen with my own eyes how brutally the Egyptians are treating them. So it's time for you to head back — I'm sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people, the Israelites, out of Egypt."
Moses said to God, "But why me? What makes you think I could ever march up to Pharaoh and lead the Israelites out of Egypt?"
"I'll be with you," God said. "And here's your proof that I'm the one sending you: once you've brought my people out of Egypt, you'll worship God right here on this very mountain."
Then Moses said to God, "OK, so I go to the Israelites and tell them, 'The God of your ancestors sent me' — and they ask, 'What's his name?' What do I tell them?"
God said to Moses, "I-AM-WHO-I-AM. Tell the Israelites: I-AM sent me to you."

God kept going: "Here's exactly what to tell the Israelites: 'God — the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob — sent me to you.' This has always been my name, and it's how I'll always be known."

"Now get moving. Gather Israel's leaders and tell them: 'God — the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — appeared to me and said: I've been paying attention to what's happening to you in Egypt, and I've decided to pull you out of your misery in Egypt and take you to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites — a land overflowing with milk and honey.'"

"Trust me, they'll listen to you. Then you and Israel's leaders will go to Egypt's king and say: 'God, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Let us take a three-day trip into the wilderness to worship God — our God.'"

"I know Egypt's king won't let you go unless he's forced — so I'll step in and hit Egypt where it really hurts. My miracles are going to leave them reeling! After that, they'll be more than happy to let you go. And I'll make sure the Egyptians treat you generously on your way out — you won't leave empty-handed! Every woman will ask her neighbor and any guests staying in her house for silver and gold items, jewelry, and extra clothes — you'll dress your sons and daughters in them. You're going to clean the Egyptians out!"
title: The Burning Bush

paragraphs: Moses pushed back: "They're not gonna trust me. They won't listen to a single word I say. They'll just laugh — 'God appeared to him? Yeah, right!'"
So God asked, "What's that in your hand?" "Just a staff," Moses said.
"Throw it on the ground." Moses threw it down — and it turned into a snake! Moses jumped back so fast!

God told Moses, "Now grab it by the tail." He reached out and grabbed it — and boom, it was his staff again. "That's how they'll know God appeared to you — the God of their ancestors, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."
Then God said, "Put your hand inside your shirt." Moses slipped his hand under his shirt and pulled it out — and his hand had turned leprous, white as snow.
God said, "Now put your hand back under your shirt." He did — and when he pulled it out, it was totally healthy again.

"So if they don't believe you after the first sign, the second one should convince them. And if they still don't trust you or listen to you after both signs — take some water from the Nile and pour it on dry ground. The moment it hits the dirt, that Nile water will turn into blood."
Moses tried another excuse on God: "Master, please — I'm terrible at speaking. I never was good with words, not before and not now either. I stutter and stammer."

God said, "Who do you think made the human mouth? Who makes people mute or deaf, sighted or blind? Isn't it me, God? So get going! I'll be right there with you — with your mouth! I'll teach you exactly what to say."
Moses said, "Oh, Master, please! Just send someone else!"

God got angry with Moses: "Don't you have a brother — Aaron the Levite? He's great with words, I know he is. He speaks really well. Actually, he's already on his way to meet you right now, and he'll be so happy to see you. You'll tell him what to say. I'll be with both of you as you speak, teaching you step by step. He'll speak to the people for you — he'll be your mouth, but you decide what comes out of it. Now pick up that staff — you're going to do the signs with it."
Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said, "I need to go back to my relatives in Egypt. I want to check if they're still alive." Jethro said, "Go — and peace be with you."
God told Moses while he was still in Midian: "Go back to Egypt. All the men who wanted you dead are dead now."
So Moses put his wife and sons on a donkey and headed back to Egypt, holding tight to the staff of God.

God told Moses, "When you get back to Egypt, get ready: all the wonders I'm going to do through you — you'll perform them right in front of Pharaoh. But I'm going to make him stubborn, so he'll refuse to let the people go. Then tell Pharaoh this message from God: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn! I told you to free my son so he can serve me. You refused. So now I'm going to kill your son — your firstborn.'"

On the way back, while they were camped for the night, God confronted Moses and was about to kill him — but Zipporah grabbed a sharp flint knife, circumcised her son, and touched Moses with the foreskin. She cried out, "You're a bridegroom of blood to me!" Then God let him go. She said "bridegroom of blood" because of the circumcision.

God told Aaron, "Go meet Moses out in the wilderness." Aaron went and met him at the mountain of God, and kissed him. Moses told Aaron everything God had sent him to say and all the wonders God had commanded him to do.

So Moses and Aaron gathered all of Israel's leaders. Aaron told them everything God had told Moses, and performed the wonders right in front of the people. The people believed — they trusted that God had seen what the Israelites were going through and knew all about their suffering. They bowed down low and worshiped.
title: Signs and Excuses

paragraphs: § Moses and Aaron and Pharaoh
After that, Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh. They said, "God, the God of Israel, says: 'Free my people so they can hold a festival for me out in the wilderness.'"
Pharaoh said, "Who is this God that I should listen to him and let Israel go? I don't know anything about this so-called 'God' — and I'm definitely not letting Israel go."
They said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Let us take a three-day journey into the wilderness to worship our God — otherwise he might strike us with disease or death."

But Egypt's king said, "Moses and Aaron, why on earth are you trying to give these people a day off? Back to work!" Pharaoh went on, "Look, I've got all these people on my hands, and now you want to reward them with time off?"

Pharaoh acted immediately. He sent orders down to the slave-drivers and their assistants: "Stop giving the people straw for making bricks like you've been doing. Make them go get their own straw. And they still have to produce the same number of bricks — no cutting their daily quota! They're just getting lazy. They keep going around saying, 'Give us time off to worship our God.' Crack down on them. That'll fix their whining and their god-fantasies."

The slave-drivers and their assistants went out and told the people the new rules: "Pharaoh's orders: no more straw for you. Go find your own straw wherever you can. And your daily brick quota doesn't drop by a single brick!" The people scattered all over Egypt, scrambling to find straw.
The slave-drivers were brutal about it: "Finish your daily quota of bricks — the same number as when we gave you straw."
The Israelite foremen that the slave-drivers had put in charge got beaten and harassed: "Why didn't you hit your brick quota yesterday or the day before — and again today?"

The Israelite foremen went to Pharaoh and begged for relief: "Why are you treating your servants like this? Nobody gives us any straw, but they order us, 'Make bricks!' Look at us — we're getting beaten, and it's not even our fault."

But Pharaoh said, "Lazy! That's what you are — lazy! That's why you're whining, 'Let us go worship God.' Fine then — go! Get back to work. Nobody's giving you straw, and by the end of the day you'd better turn in your full quota of bricks."
The Israelite foremen realized they were in deep trouble, having to go back and tell their workers, "Not one brick short of your daily quota."

As they were leaving Pharaoh, they ran into Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them. The foremen said, "May God see what you've done and judge you — you've made us stink in front of Pharaoh and his servants! You've handed him a weapon that's going to kill us!"

Moses went back to God and said, "My Master, why are you treating these people so badly? Why did you even send me? Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in your name, things have only gotten worse for these people. And rescue? Does this look like a rescue to you?"
title: Bricks Without Straw

paragraphs: God said to Moses, "Now you're going to see what I'll do to Pharaoh: with a strong hand he'll send them out free — with a strong hand he'll drive them out of his land."

God kept talking to Moses, reassuring him: "I am God. I showed up to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as The Strong God, but they didn't know me by my name God — I-Am-Present. I also made my covenant with them, promising to give them the land of Canaan, the country where they lived as outsiders. But now I've heard the Israelites groaning under the Egyptians who keep enslaving them, and I've remembered my covenant. So here's what to tell the Israelites:

"I am God. I will bring you out from under Egypt's cruel, crushing labor. I will rescue you from slavery. I will redeem you with powerful acts of judgment. I'll take you as my own people, and I'll be your God. Then you'll know that I am God — your God — the one who brings you out from under Egypt's cruel labor. I'll bring you into the land I promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and give it to you as your own country. I AM God."
But when Moses gave this message to the Israelites, they couldn't even hear him — they were that crushed in spirit by the brutal slave conditions.
Then God said to Moses, "Go talk to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and get him to release the Israelites from his land."
Moses answered God, "Look — the Israelites won't even listen to me. How do you expect Pharaoh to listen? And besides, I stutter."
But God laid out the facts again to Moses and Aaron — about the Israelites and about Pharaoh, king of Egypt — and he commanded them again to lead the Israelites out of Egypt.
§ The Family Tree of Moses and Aaron
These are the heads of the tribes. The sons of Reuben, Israel's firstborn: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi — these are the families of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jakin, Zohar, and Saul, the son of a Canaanite woman — these are the families of Simeon.
These are the names of Levi's sons, in birth order: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years.
The sons of Gershon, by family: Libni and Shimei.
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived to be 133.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are Levi's sons, in birth order.
Amram married his aunt Jochebed, and she gave birth to Aaron and Moses. Amram lived to be 137.
The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zicri.
The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
Aaron married Elisheba — the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon — and she gave birth to Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the Korahite families.
Aaron's son Eleazar married one of Putiel's daughters, and she gave birth to Phinehas. These are the heads of the Levite families, family by family.

This is the Aaron and Moses God commanded: "Bring the Israelites out of Egypt, clan by clan." These are the men — Moses and Aaron — who told Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to release the Israelites from Egypt.
§ "I'll Make You as a God to Pharaoh"
And that's how things stood when God spoke to Moses in Egypt again.
God said to Moses, "I am God. Tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, everything I tell you."
And Moses answered, "Look at me — I stutter. Why would Pharaoh listen to me?"

paragraphs: God told Moses, "Look at me. I'm going to make you like a god to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet. You speak everything I command you, and your brother Aaron will say it to Pharaoh — then he'll let the Israelites go from his land. At the same time, I'm going to make Pharaoh dig in his heels, and then I'll fill Egypt with signs and wonders. Pharaoh won't listen to you, but I'll have my way with Egypt and bring out my army — my people, the Israelites — from Egypt with mighty acts of judgment. The Egyptians will know that I am God when I step in and pull the Israelites out of their country."
Moses and Aaron did exactly what God commanded. Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.
Then God spoke to Moses and Aaron: "When Pharaoh says to you, 'Prove yourselves — do a miracle,' tell Aaron, 'Take your staff and throw it down in front of Pharaoh — it will turn into a snake.'"
Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did what God commanded. Aaron threw his staff down in front of Pharaoh and his servants, and it turned into a snake.

Pharaoh called in his wise men and sorcerers. Egypt's magicians did the same thing with their spells — each one threw down his staff and they all turned into snakes. But then Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.
Still, Pharaoh was as stubborn as ever — he wouldn't listen to them, just as God had said.
§ Strike One: Blood

God said to Moses: "Pharaoh is a stubborn man. He refuses to let the people go. First thing tomorrow morning, go meet Pharaoh as he heads down to the river. Take the staff that turned into a snake and stand at the edge of the Nile, and say to him: 'God, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you with this message: Release my people so they can worship me in the wilderness. You haven't listened so far. This is how you'll know that I am God: I'm going to take this staff in my hand and strike the water of the Nile — the water will turn to blood, the fish in the Nile will die, the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians won't be able to drink the Nile water.'"

God said to Moses, "Tell Aaron: 'Take your staff and wave it over the waters of Egypt — over its rivers, its canals, its ponds, every body of water — so they all turn to blood.' There'll be blood everywhere in Egypt — even in the pots and pans."

Moses and Aaron did exactly as God commanded. With Pharaoh and his servants watching, Aaron raised his staff and struck the water of the Nile. All the water in the Nile turned to blood. The fish in the Nile died, the Nile stank, and the Egyptians couldn't drink the Nile water. Blood was everywhere in Egypt.

But Egypt's magicians did the same thing with their magic spells. Pharaoh stayed stubborn. He wouldn't listen to them, just as God had said. He turned around and went home, not giving it a second thought. Meanwhile all the Egyptians had to dig near the river for drinking water, since they couldn't drink the Nile water. Seven days passed after God struck the Nile.

paragraphs: § Strike Two: Frogs

God said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him: God's Message — Release my people so they can worship me. If you refuse, I'm warning you: I'll hit the whole country with frogs. The Nile will swarm with frogs — they'll crawl into your houses, your bedrooms, your beds, your servants' rooms, all over the people, into your ovens and your pots and pans. They'll be all over you — frogs everywhere, on and in everything!"
God told Moses, "Tell Aaron: wave your staff over the rivers, canals, and ponds. Bring frogs up over Egypt."
Aaron stretched his staff over the waters of Egypt, and a huge mob of frogs came up and covered the whole country.
But the magicians did the same thing with their magic spells — they also brought frogs up over Egypt.
Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron in and said, "Pray to God to get rid of these frogs. I'll let the people go so they can sacrifice and worship God."
Moses said to Pharaoh, "Sure. You set the time — when do you want the frogs gone from you, your servants, your people, and your houses? You'll be rid of frogs, except the ones in the Nile."

"Make it tomorrow." Moses said, "Tomorrow it is — so you'll know there's no God like our God. The frogs will be gone — you, your houses, your servants, your people, all frog-free. The only frogs left will be in the Nile."

Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, and Moses prayed to God about the frogs he'd brought on Pharaoh. God answered Moses' prayer: the frogs died — houses, courtyards, fields, all frog-free. They piled the dead frogs in heaps, and the whole country stank of dead frogs.
But when Pharaoh saw he'd gotten some breathing room, he got stubborn again and wouldn't listen to Moses and Aaron. Just as God had said.
§ Strike Three: Gnats
God told Moses, "Tell Aaron: take your staff and strike the dust — the dust will turn into gnats all over Egypt."

He did it. Aaron grabbed his staff and struck the dust of the ground — it turned into gnats, gnats all over people and animals. All the dust of the ground turned into gnats, gnats everywhere in Egypt.
The magicians tried to make gnats with their spells, but this time they couldn't. Gnats were everywhere, all over people and animals.
The magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is God's doing." But Pharaoh was stubborn and wouldn't listen. Just as God had said.
§ Strike Four: Flies

God told Moses, "Get up early in the morning and confront Pharaoh as he goes down to the water. Tell him: God's Message — Release my people so they can worship me. If you don't release my people, I'll send swarms of flies on you, your servants, your people, and your houses. The Egyptians' houses — even the ground under their feet — will be thick with flies. But when it happens, I'll set Goshen apart as a safe zone, where my people live — no flies in Goshen. That'll prove I'm God, right here in this land. I'll make a sharp line between your people and mine. This sign happens tomorrow."
And God did exactly that. Thick swarms of flies filled Pharaoh's palace and his servants' houses. All over Egypt, the country was being wrecked by flies.
Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron in and said, "Fine, go. Sacrifice to your God — but do it here, in this country."

Moses said, "That wouldn't be smart. What we sacrifice to our God would deeply offend the Egyptians. If we openly sacrifice what offends them so much, they'll kill us. Let us go on a three-day journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to our God, just like he told us."
Pharaoh said, "OK. I'll let you go sacrifice to your God in the wilderness. Just don't go too far. And pray for me."
Moses said, "The moment I leave, I'll pray to God that tomorrow the flies leave you, your servants, and your people. But don't trick us and change your mind about letting us go sacrifice to God."

Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to God. God did what Moses asked — he got rid of the flies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. Not a single fly was left. But Pharaoh got stubborn again and wouldn't let the people go.
title: Strikes Two, Three, Four: Frogs, Gnats, Flies

paragraphs: § Strike Five: Animals

God told Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and say: God, the God of the Hebrews, says — Release my people so they can worship me. If you refuse and keep holding on to them, here's fair warning: God will hit your livestock out in the fields hard — horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, sheep — with a terrible disease. God will draw a sharp line between Israel's livestock and Egypt's livestock. Not a single animal belonging to the Israelites will die."
Then God set the time: "Tomorrow, God will do this."

The next day, God did it. All of Egypt's livestock died — but not one Israelite animal died. Pharaoh sent men to check, and sure enough: none of the Israelites' livestock had died — not a single one. But Pharaoh stayed stubborn. He wouldn't let the people go.
§ Strike Six: Boils

God told Moses and Aaron, "Grab handfuls of soot from a furnace, and have Moses toss it into the air right in front of Pharaoh. It'll become a fine dust all over Egypt and cause painful sores — boils erupting on people and animals all over Egypt." So they took soot from a furnace, stood in front of Pharaoh, and threw it into the air. Boils erupted on people and animals. The magicians couldn't even stand up to Moses this time because of the boils — they were covered in boils just like everyone else in Egypt.
God hardened Pharaoh's stubborn heart. He wouldn't listen, just as God had told Moses.
§ Strike Seven: Hail

God told Moses, "Get up early in the morning and confront Pharaoh. Tell him: God, the God of the Hebrews, says — Release my people so they can worship me. This time I'm going to hit you, your servants, and your people with the full force of my power, so you'll finally get it: there's no one like me anywhere on earth. You know I could have struck you and your people with a deadly plague by now, and you'd be wiped out — not a trace left. But I've kept you standing for one reason only: to show you my power, so my name gets famous all over the earth. You're still pushing my people down to build yourself up. You're not letting them go. So here's what's coming: tomorrow at this time, I'm sending a massive hailstorm — nothing like it has ever hit Egypt since the day it was founded. So get your livestock under cover — everything left out in the open fields, people and animals, will die when the hail falls."

All of Pharaoh's servants who respected God's word rushed to get their workers and animals under cover as fast as they could — but the ones who didn't take God's word seriously left their workers and animals out in the fields.
God told Moses, "Stretch your hands toward the sky. Signal the hail to fall all over Egypt — on people, animals, and crops out in Egypt's fields."

Moses raised his staff to the sky, and God sent thunder cracks and hail mixed with lightning strikes. God rained hail down on Egypt. The hail came down — hail and lightning, a brutal hailstorm. Nothing like it had ever happened in Egypt in its entire history. The hail pounded all of Egypt. Everything out in the open fields — people, animals, crops — got smashed. Even the trees in the fields were shattered. The only exception: Goshen, where the Israelites lived. No hail in Goshen.

Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron. He said, "I admit it — I really sinned this time. God is right, and I and my people are wrong. Pray to God. We've had enough of God's thunder and hail. I'll let you go — the sooner you're out of here, the better."

Moses said, "As soon as I'm out of the city, I'll stretch my arms out to God. The thunder will stop and the hail will end, so you'll know the earth belongs to God. But I know you and your servants still don't respect God."
(The flax and barley were destroyed — they were just ripening — but the wheat and spelt survived, since they ripen later.)
Moses left Pharaoh and the city, stretched his arms out to God. The thunder and hail stopped; the storm cleared.

But when Pharaoh saw the rain, hail, and thunder had stopped, he kept on sinning — stubborn as ever, him and his servants. Pharaoh's heart turned rock-hard. He refused to release the Israelites, just as God had said through Moses.
title: Strikes Five, Six, Seven: Animals, Boils, Hail

paragraphs: § Strike Eight: Locusts

God said to Moses: "Go to Pharaoh. I've made him — and his servants — stubborn, so I can force him to face these signs, and so you'll be able to tell your children and grandchildren how I toyed with the Egyptians like a cat with a mouse. You'll tell them the stories of the signs I brought down on them, so you'll all know that I am God."

Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, "God, the God of the Hebrews, says: 'How long are you going to refuse to bow down? Release my people so they can worship me. If you refuse to release my people, watch out — tomorrow I'm bringing locusts into your country. They'll cover every inch of ground; no one will even see the dirt. They'll eat everything the hail left behind — even the young trees out in the fields, they'll strip the trees bare. They'll invade your houses, filling your servants' houses, filling every house in Egypt. No one has ever seen anything like this, from the time your ancestors first stepped onto this land until today.'" Then he turned on his heel and walked out on Pharaoh.
Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long are you going to let this guy wreck us? Let these people go worship their God. Can't you see Egypt is finished?"
So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. He said to them, "Fine, go ahead. Go worship your God. But exactly who is going with you?"
Moses said, "We're taking everyone — young and old, our sons and daughters, our flocks and herds. This is our worship celebration for God."

He said, "I'd sooner let you go with God's blessing than let you take your children. Look — you're up to no good, it's written all over your faces. No way. Only the men go — go worship God, since that's what you want so badly." And they were thrown out of Pharaoh's presence.
God said to Moses: "Stretch your hand over Egypt and signal the locusts to cover Egypt, eating every blade of grass in the country — everything the hail didn't destroy."
Moses stretched his staff over Egypt. God sent an east wind. It blew all day and all night. By morning, the east wind had brought the locusts.

The locusts covered the whole country of Egypt, settling over every inch of Egypt — the place was crawling with locusts. There had never been a locust invasion like it before, and there never will be again. The ground was completely covered, black with locusts. They ate everything — every blade of grass, every piece of fruit, anything the hail hadn't destroyed. Nothing was left but bare trees and bare fields — not a speck of green anywhere in Egypt.

Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron in a hurry. He said, "I've sinned against your God and against you. Forgive my sin just one more time. Pray to your God to get me out of this — get this death away from here!"
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to God. God flipped the wind around — a powerful west wind picked up the locusts and dumped them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust was left anywhere in Egypt.
But God made Pharaoh stubborn as ever. He still wouldn't release the Israelites.
§ Strike Nine: Darkness
God said to Moses: "Stretch your hand toward the sky. Let darkness fall on Egypt — a darkness so thick you can feel it."

Moses stretched his hand toward the sky. Thick darkness fell over Egypt for three days. Nobody could see anyone. For three days, no one could even move. Except the Israelites — they had light where they lived.
Pharaoh called Moses in: "Go worship God. Leave your flocks and herds behind. But take your children with you."

But Moses said, "You have to let us take our sacrificial animals and offerings with us, so we can sacrifice them in worship to our God. All our livestock has to come with us — not a single hoof left behind. They're part of how we worship our God. And we won't know exactly what we'll need until we get there."
But God kept Pharaoh stubborn as ever. He wouldn't agree to let them go.
Pharaoh said to Moses: "Get out of my sight! Watch yourself. I never want to see you again. If I see your face again, you're dead."
Moses said, "Have it your way. You won't see my face again."
title: Strikes Eight and Nine: Locusts and Darkness

paragraphs: § Strike Ten: Death

God said to Moses: "I'm going to hit Pharaoh and Egypt one final time — and then he'll let you go. When he lets you go, that'll be the end of Egypt for you — he won't be able to get rid of you fast enough."

"So here's what to do: tell the people to ask their neighbors — every man from his neighbor, every woman from her neighbor — for silver and gold items." God made sure the Egyptians looked kindly on the people. And Moses himself was hugely respected by the Egyptians — a major public figure among Pharaoh's servants and the people.

Then Moses confronted Pharaoh: "God's Message: Tonight at midnight I will go through Egypt, and every firstborn in Egypt will die — from Pharaoh's firstborn, sitting on his throne, to the firstborn of the slave girl working at her hand mill. Even the firstborn of the animals. Wailing will break out all over the country — grief like never before and never again. But among the Israelites — man, woman, or animal — there won't be so much as a dog barking, so you'll know that God draws a clear line between Egypt and Israel."
"Then all these servants of yours will come groveling to me, begging, 'Leave! You and everyone who follows you!' And I will absolutely leave." Moses, burning with anger, walked out on Pharaoh.
God told Moses, "Pharaoh won't listen to a word you say — so that the signs of my presence and power will multiply in Egypt."
Moses and Aaron had performed all these signs in front of Pharaoh, but God made Pharaoh more stubborn than ever — once again, he refused to release the Israelites from his land.

paragraphs: God spoke to Moses and Aaron while they were still in Egypt: "This month is month number one for you — the first month of your year. Tell the whole Israelite community: on the tenth day of this month, each man takes a lamb for his family — one lamb per household. If a family is too small for a whole lamb, share one with a close neighbor — figure it out based on how many people there are and how much each person eats. Your lamb has to be a healthy one-year-old male — pick it from the sheep or the goats. Keep it penned up until the fourteenth day of the month, then slaughter it — the whole Israelite community does this — at dusk. Then take some of the blood and smear it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the house where you'll eat it. That night, eat the meat roasted over fire, with bread made without yeast and bitter herbs. Don't eat any of it raw or boiled — make sure it's roasted, the whole animal: head, legs, and insides. Don't leave any of it till morning; burn whatever's left in the fire."
"And here's how to eat it: fully dressed, sandals on, walking stick in hand. Eat in a hurry — this is God's Passover."

"Tonight I will go through Egypt and strike down every firstborn in Egypt — human or animal — and bring judgment on all the gods of Egypt. I am God. The blood will be a sign on your houses. When I see the blood, I will pass over you — no disaster will touch you when I strike Egypt."

"This will be a memorial day for you — celebrate it as a festival to God for generations to come, a permanent festival, always. For seven days you'll eat unraised bread (matzoth): on day one, get all the yeast out of your houses — anyone who eats anything with yeast from day one to day seven will be cut off from Israel. Days one and seven are holy — no work on those days. Only what you need to do for meals — that's allowed."

"Keep the Festival of Unraised Bread! This marks the exact day I brought you out of Egypt in full force. Honor this day for generations — a permanent festival, always. From the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month until the evening of the twenty-first day, eat unraised bread. For those seven days, not a speck of yeast anywhere in your houses. Anyone — visitor or native — who eats anything raised will be cut off from the Israelite community. Don't eat anything raised. Only matzoth."

Moses gathered all Israel's elders. He said, "Pick a lamb for your families and slaughter the Passover lamb. Take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the bowl of blood, and smear it on the lintel and the two doorposts. Nobody leaves the house until morning. God will pass through to strike Egypt down. When he sees the blood on the lintel and the two doorposts, God will pass over the doorway — he won't let the destroyer come into your house to wreck you."

"Keep this word — it's the law for you and your children, forever. When you enter the land God promised to give you, keep doing this. And when your children ask, 'Why are we doing this?' tell them: 'It's the Passover sacrifice to God, who passed over the Israelites' homes in Egypt when he hit Egypt with death but rescued us.'" The people bowed down and worshiped.
Then the Israelites went and did what God had commanded Moses and Aaron. They did all of it.
At midnight, God struck every firstborn in Egypt — from Pharaoh's firstborn on his throne down to the firstborn of the prisoner locked in jail. And the firstborn of the animals too.
Pharaoh got up that night — him, all his servants, everyone in Egypt — and wild wailing broke out all over Egypt! There wasn't a single house without someone dead.

Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron in that very night and said, "Get out of here — you and your Israelites, I'm done with you! Go worship God on your own terms. And yes, take your sheep and cattle like you've been insisting — just go. And bless me."
The Egyptians couldn't wait to get rid of them — they pushed them to hurry: "We're all as good as dead!"

The people grabbed their bread dough before it could rise, wrapped their bread bowls in their cloaks, and slung them over their shoulders. The Israelites had already done what Moses told them — they'd asked the Egyptians for silver and gold items and clothing. God made sure the Egyptians liked the people, so they readily gave them whatever they asked for. Oh yes — they cleaned those Egyptians out.

The Israelites traveled from Rameses to Succoth — about 600,000 men on foot, plus their families. Hebrews and non-Hebrews alike set out, along with huge flocks and herds of livestock. They baked flat unraised cakes from the dough they'd brought out of Egypt — it hadn't risen because they'd been rushed out of Egypt with no time to prepare food for the trip.
§ The Passover

The Israelites had lived in Egypt 430 years. At the end of those 430 years — to the very day — God's whole army left Egypt. God stayed awake all night, watching over the Israelites as he brought them out of Egypt. Because God kept watch, all Israel for all generations will honor God by keeping watch this night — a watchnight.

God told Moses and Aaron, "Here are the Passover rules: no foreigners eat it. Any slave who's been bought and circumcised can eat it. No casual visitor or hired worker can eat it. Eat it in one house — don't take the meat outside. Don't break any of its bones. The whole Israelite community joins in the meal."

"If an immigrant living with you wants to keep God's Passover, every male in his family must be circumcised — then he can join the meal, treated as a native son. But no uncircumcised person can eat it."
"The same law applies to the native and the immigrant living with you."
All the Israelites did exactly as God commanded Moses and Aaron. That very day, God brought the Israelites out of Egypt, tribe by tribe.
title: The Passover

paragraphs: God spoke to Moses, saying, "Set apart every firstborn for me — the first one out of the womb among the Israelites, whether person or animal, is mine."
Moses said to the people, "Always remember this day. This is the day you came out of Egypt, out of a house of slavery. God brought you out of here with a powerful hand. Don't eat any raised bread."

"You are leaving in the spring month of Abib. When God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites — which he promised your fathers to give you, a land overflowing with milk and honey — you are to keep this service in this month:"
"Eat unraised bread for seven days; on the seventh day there's a festival celebration to God."
"Only unraised bread is to be eaten for seven days. There must not be a trace of anything fermented — no yeast anywhere."
"Tell your child on that day: 'This is because of what God did for me when I came out of Egypt.'"

"The day you keep will be like a sign on your hand, a memorial between your eyes, and God's teaching in your mouth. It was with a powerful hand that God brought you out of Egypt. Keep these instructions at the set time, year after year after year."

"When God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he promised you and your fathers, and hands it over to you, set aside the first birth out of every womb for God. Every first birth from your livestock belongs to God. You can redeem the first birth of a donkey if you want by swapping in a lamb; if you decide not to redeem it, you must break its neck."

"Redeem every firstborn son among your sons. When the time comes and your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' tell him, 'God brought us out of Egypt, out of a house of slavery, with a powerful hand. When Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, God killed every firstborn in Egypt — firstborn of humans and animals alike. That's why I sacrifice every first male birth from the womb to God and redeem every firstborn son.' The observance works like a sign on your hands or a symbol on the middle of your forehead: God brought us out of Egypt with a powerful hand."

It so happened that after Pharaoh released the people, God didn't lead them by the road through Philistine country — the shortest route — because God thought, "If the people run into war, they'll change their minds and go back to Egypt."
So God led the people by the wilderness road, looping around to the Red Sea. The Israelites left Egypt in military formation.
Moses took Joseph's bones with him, because Joseph had made the Israelites solemnly swear to do it, saying, "God will surely hold you accountable, so make sure you bring my bones from here with you."

They moved on from Succoth and camped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness. God went ahead of them in a Pillar of Cloud by day to guide them on the way, and by night in a Pillar of Fire to give them light — so they could travel day and night. The Pillar of Cloud by day and the Pillar of Fire by night never left the people.

paragraphs: § The Story and Song of Salvation
God spoke to Moses: "Tell the Israelites to turn around and camp at Pi Hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. Camp by the sea, opposite Baal Zephon."

"Pharaoh will think, 'The Israelites are lost — they're confused. The wilderness has closed in on them.' Then I'll make Pharaoh stubborn again and he'll chase after them. And I'll use Pharaoh and his army to put my Glory on display. Then the Egyptians will realize that I am God." And that's what happened.

When the king of Egypt was told the people were gone, he and his servants changed their minds. They said, "What have we done, letting Israel — our slave labor — go free?" So he had his chariots harnessed and gathered his army. He took six hundred of his best chariots, with the rest of Egypt's chariots and their drivers coming along.

God made Pharaoh, king of Egypt, stubborn — determined to chase the Israelites as they walked out on him without even looking back. The Egyptians chased them and caught up with them where they'd camped by the sea — all of Pharaoh's horse-drawn chariots and riders, all his foot soldiers, there at Pi Hahiroth opposite Baal Zephon.

As Pharaoh got closer, the Israelites looked up and saw them — Egyptians! Coming at them! They were terrified. They cried out in terror to God. They told Moses, "Weren't there enough cemeteries in Egypt that you had to drag us out here into the wilderness to die? What have you done to us, bringing us out of Egypt? Didn't we tell you back in Egypt this would happen? Didn't we say, 'Leave us alone in Egypt — we're better off as slaves in Egypt than as corpses in the wilderness'?"
Moses spoke to the people: "Don't be afraid. Stand firm and watch God do his saving work for you today. Take a good look at the Egyptians today — you're never going to see them again."
"God will fight the battle for you. And you? Keep your mouths shut!"

God said to Moses: "Why are you crying out to me? Talk to the Israelites. Order them to get moving. Hold your staff high and stretch your hand out over the sea: Split the sea! The Israelites will walk through the sea on dry ground."

"Meanwhile, I'll make sure the Egyptians keep up their stubborn chase — I'll use Pharaoh and his whole army, his chariots and horsemen, to put my Glory on display, so the Egyptians will realize that I am God."

The angel of God that had been leading Israel's camp now shifted and got behind them. And the Pillar of Cloud that had been in front also shifted to the rear. The Cloud stood between Egypt's camp and Israel's camp. The Cloud wrapped one camp in darkness and flooded the other with light. The two camps didn't come near each other all night.
Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and God — with a powerful east wind blowing all night long — pushed the sea back. He made the sea dry ground. The waters split.

The Israelites walked through the sea on dry ground, the waters like a wall to their right and to their left. The Egyptians came after them in full pursuit — every horse, chariot, and driver of Pharaoh racing into the middle of the sea. It was now the morning watch. God looked down from the Pillar of Fire and Cloud on the Egyptian army and threw them into a panic. He jammed the wheels of their chariots — they were stuck in the mud. The Egyptians said, "Run from Israel! God is fighting for them and against Egypt!"
God said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, and the waters will come back over the Egyptians — over their chariots, over their horsemen."

Moses stretched his hand out over the sea: as day broke and the Egyptians were running, the sea returned to its place as before. God dumped the Egyptians into the middle of the sea. The waters came back, drowning Pharaoh's chariots and riders — the whole army that had chased Israel into the sea. Not one of them survived.

But the Israelites walked right through the middle of the sea on dry ground, the waters forming a wall to the right and to the left. God rescued Israel that day from the Egyptians' grip. And Israel looked at the Egyptian dead, washed up on the seashore, and realized the tremendous power God had unleashed against the Egyptians. The people stood in reverent awe before God and trusted in God and his servant Moses.
title: The Red Sea

paragraphs: Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to God, singing it out together: I'm singing my heart out to God — what a victory! He threw horse and rider into the sea. God is my strength, God is my song, and yes! God is my salvation. This is the kind of God I have, and I'm telling the world! This is my father's God — I'm spreading the news everywhere! God is a fighter, pure God through and through. Pharaoh's chariots and army he dumped in the sea; the elite of his officers he drowned in the Red Sea. Wild ocean waters poured over them; they sank like a rock in the deep blue sea. Your strong right hand, God, shimmers with power; your strong right hand shatters the enemy. In your mighty majesty you smash your arrogant enemies; you let loose your hot anger and burn them to a crisp. At a blast from your nostrils the waters piled up; tumbling streams dammed up, wild oceans curdled into a swamp.
The enemy bragged, "I'll chase them, I'll hunt them down, I'll divide up the loot, I'll stuff myself on them; I'll pull out my sword, my fist will send them reeling."

You blew with all your might and the sea covered them. They sank like a lead weight in the majestic waters. Who compares with you among the gods, O God? Who compares with you in power, in holy majesty, in awesome praises, wonder-working God?
You stretched out your right hand and the earth swallowed them up. But the people you redeemed, you led in merciful love; you guided them under your protection to your holy pasture.

When the nations heard, they were scared; Philistines writhed and trembled; yes, even the chiefs in Edom were shaken, and the big bosses in Moab. Everyone in Canaan panicked and went limp. Dread and terror sent them reeling. Before your raised right arm they stood dumb like a stone — until your people crossed over and entered, O God, until the people you made crossed over and entered. You brought them and planted them on the mountain of your heritage, the place where you live, the place you made, your sanctuary, Master, that you established with your own hands. Let God rule forever, for eternity!
Yes, Pharaoh's horses and chariots and riders went into the sea and God turned the waters back on them; but the Israelites walked on dry land right through the middle of the sea.

Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine, and all the women followed her with tambourines, dancing. Miriam led them in singing: Sing to God — what a victory! He threw horse and rider into the sea!
§ Traveling Through the Wilderness

Moses led Israel from the Red Sea on to the Wilderness of Shur. They traveled three days through the wilderness without finding any water. They got to Marah, but they couldn't drink the water at Marah — it was bitter. That's why they called the place Marah (Bitter). And the people complained to Moses, "So what are we supposed to drink?"
So Moses cried out in prayer to God. God pointed him to a piece of wood. Moses threw it into the water and the water turned sweet.

That's the place where God set up rules and procedures; that's where he started testing them. God said, "If you listen — really listen to how God tells you to live in his presence — obey his commands and keep all his laws, then I won't strike you with any of the diseases I hit the Egyptians with; I am God, your healer."
They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. They camped there by the water.

paragraphs: On the fifteenth day of the second month after leaving Egypt, the whole Israelite company moved on from Elim to the Wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai. The whole company of Israel complained against Moses and Aaron there in the wilderness. The Israelites said, "Why didn't God just let us die comfortably in Egypt, where we had lamb stew and all the bread we could eat? You've dragged us out into this wilderness to starve the whole company of Israel to death!"

God said to Moses, "I'm going to rain bread down from the skies for you. The people will go out and gather each day's ration. I'm going to test them to see if they'll live by my teaching or not. On the sixth day, when they prepare what they've gathered, it'll turn out to be twice as much as their daily ration."

Moses and Aaron told the People of Israel, "This evening you'll know that it is God who brought you out of Egypt; and in the morning you'll see the Glory of God. Yes, he's heard your complaints against him. You haven't been complaining against us, you know — but against God."

Moses said, "Since it will be God who gives you meat for dinner in the evening and your fill of bread in the morning, it's God who has heard your complaints against him. Who are we in all this? You haven't been complaining to us — you've been complaining to God!"
Moses told Aaron: "Tell the whole company of Israel: 'Come near to God. He's heard your complaints.'"
When Aaron gave the instructions to the whole company of Israel, they turned to face the wilderness. And there it was: the Glory of God, visible in the Cloud.
God spoke to Moses, "I've heard the Israelites' complaints. Now tell them: 'At dusk you'll eat meat, and at dawn you'll eat your fill of bread; and you'll realize that I am God, your God.'"

That evening quail flew in and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew all over the camp. When the layer of dew lifted, there on the wilderness ground was a fine flaky something, fine as frost on the ground. The Israelites took one look and said to one another, man-hu (What is it?). They had no idea what it was.

So Moses told them, "It's the bread God has given you to eat. And these are God's instructions: 'Gather enough for each person — about two quarts per person; gather enough for everyone in your tent.'"

The People of Israel went to work and started gathering, some more, some less, but when they measured out what they'd gathered, those who gathered more had no extra and those who gathered less weren't short — each person had gathered exactly what was needed.
Moses said to them, "Don't leave any of it until morning."
But they didn't listen to Moses. A few of the men kept some back until morning. It got wormy and smelled awful. And Moses lost his temper with them.

They gathered it every morning, each person according to need. Then the sun heated up and it melted. On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread — about four quarts per person. Then the leaders of the company came to Moses and reported.

Moses said, "This is what God was talking about: Tomorrow is a day of rest, a holy Sabbath to God. Whatever you plan to bake, bake today; whatever you plan to boil, boil today. Then set aside the leftovers until morning." They set aside what was left until morning, as Moses had commanded. It didn't smell bad and there were no worms in it.

Moses said, "Eat it now; today is a Sabbath day for God. You won't find any of it on the ground today. Gather it six days a week, but the seventh day is Sabbath — there won't be any of it on the ground."
On the seventh day, some of the people went out to gather anyway, but they didn't find anything.

God said to Moses, "How long are you going to disobey my commands and ignore my instructions? Don't you see that God has given you the Sabbath? So on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. So each of you stay home. Don't leave home on the seventh day."
So the people stopped working on the seventh day.
The Israelites named it manna (What is it?). It looked like coriander seed, whitish. And it tasted like a cracker with honey.
Moses said, "This is God's command: 'Keep a two-quart jar of it — an omer — for future generations, so they can see the bread I fed you in the wilderness after I brought you out of Egypt.'"
Moses told Aaron, "Take a jar and fill it with two quarts of manna. Place it before God, keeping it safe for future generations."
Aaron did what God commanded Moses. He set it aside before the Testimony to preserve it.
The Israelites ate the manna for forty years, until they arrived at the land where they would settle. They ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan.
By ancient measurements, an omer is one-tenth of an ephah.

The people picked a fight with Moses: "Give us water to drink." But Moses said, "Why are you pestering me? Why are you testing God?"
But the people were dying of thirst there. They complained to Moses, "Why did you drag us out of Egypt — us, our children, our animals — to die of thirst out here?"
Moses cried out in prayer to God, "What am I supposed to do with these people? Any minute now they'll kill me!"

God said to Moses, "Go on out ahead of the people, taking some of Israel's elders with you. Take the staff you used to strike the Nile. And go. I'm going to stand before you there on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock. Water will gush out of it and the people will drink."

Amalek came and fought Israel at Rephidim. Moses ordered Joshua: "Pick some men for us and go out and fight Amalek. Tomorrow I'll stand on top of the hill, holding God's staff."

Joshua did what Moses ordered, to fight Amalek. And Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. It turned out that whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel was winning, but whenever he lowered his hands, Amalek was winning. But Moses' hands got tired. So they got a stone and put it under him. He sat on it, and Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on each side. So his hands stayed steady until the sun went down. Joshua defeated Amalek and its army in battle.
God said to Moses, "Write this up as a reminder to Joshua — keep it in front of him — because I will absolutely wipe the very memory of Amalek off the face of the earth."
Moses built an altar and named it "God My Banner." He said: Salute God's rule! God at war with Amalek — always and forever!

paragraphs: Jethro, priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law, heard all the reports of what God had done for Moses and Israel his people — the news that God had delivered Israel from Egypt. Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had taken in Zipporah, Moses' wife, who had been sent back home, along with her two sons. One was named Gershom (Sojourner), because Moses had said, "I'm a sojourner in a foreign land"; the other's name was Eliezer (God's-Help), because "The God of my father is my help and saved me from death by Pharaoh."

Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, brought Moses his sons and his wife there in the wilderness, where he was camped at the mountain of God. He had sent a message ahead to Moses: "I, your father-in-law, am coming to you with your wife and two sons."

Moses went out to welcome his father-in-law. He bowed to him and kissed him. Each asked the other how things had been. Then they went into the tent. Moses told his father-in-law the whole story of what God had done to Pharaoh and Egypt for Israel's sake — all the trouble they'd run into on the journey, and how God had delivered them.

Jethro was delighted at all the good God had done for Israel in delivering them from Egyptian oppression. Jethro said, "Blessed be God, who delivered you from the power of Egypt and Pharaoh — who delivered his people from Egyptian oppression. Now I know that God is greater than all gods, because he's done this to all those who treated Israel arrogantly."
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, brought a Whole-Burnt-Offering and sacrifices to God. And Aaron, along with all Israel's elders, came and ate the meal with Moses' father-in-law in God's presence.

The next day Moses took his place to judge the people. People stood before him all day long, from morning to night. When Moses' father-in-law saw all he was doing for the people, he said, "What's going on here? Why are you doing all this by yourself, with everybody lined up before you from morning to night?"

Moses told his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me with questions about God. When something comes up, they come to me. I judge between a man and his neighbor, and I teach them God's laws and instructions."

Moses' father-in-law said, "This is no way to do it. You'll burn out — and the people with you. This is way too much for you; you can't do it alone. Now listen to me. Let me tell you how to do this so God will be in it with you. Be there for the people before God, but bring the hard questions to God. Your job is to teach them the rules and instructions — show them how to live, what to do. And then keep a sharp eye out for capable men — men who fear God, men of integrity, men who can't be bought — and appoint them as leaders over groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. They'll handle the everyday judging among the people. They'll bring the hard cases to you, but they'll judge the routine cases themselves. They'll share your load, and that'll make it easier for you. If you work this way, you'll have the strength to carry out whatever God commands you, and the people in their settings will flourish too."

Moses listened to his father-in-law's advice and did everything he said. Moses picked capable men from all Israel and set them as leaders over the people, organized by thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. They took over the everyday judging among the people. They brought the hard cases to Moses, but they judged the routine cases themselves. Then Moses said goodbye to his father-in-law, who went home to his own country.
title: Jethro's Advice

paragraphs: § Mount Sinai

Three months after leaving Egypt, the Israelites entered the Wilderness of Sinai. They traveled on from Rephidim, arrived at the Wilderness of Sinai, and set up camp. Israel camped there facing the mountain.

As Moses went up to meet God, God called down to him from the mountain: "Speak to the House of Jacob, tell the People of Israel: 'You have seen what I did to Egypt and how I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to me. If you will listen obediently to what I say and keep my covenant, out of all peoples you'll be my special treasure. The whole earth is mine to choose from, but you're special: a kingdom of priests, a holy nation.' This is what I want you to tell the People of Israel."
Moses came back and called Israel's elders together and laid out before them all these words God had commanded him.
The people answered with one voice: "Everything God says, we will do." Moses took the people's answer back to God.
God said to Moses, "Get ready. I'm about to come to you in a thick cloud, so the people can listen in and trust you completely when I speak with you." Again Moses reported the people's answer to God.

God said to Moses, "Go to the people. For the next two days, get these people ready to meet the Holy God. Have them scrub their clothes, so that on the third day they'll be fully prepared — because on the third day God will come down on Mount Sinai and make his presence known to all the people. Post boundaries for the people all around, telling them, 'Warning! Don't climb the mountain. Don't even touch its edge. Whoever touches the mountain dies — a certain death. And no one is to touch that person — he's to be stoned. That's right — stoned. Or shot with arrows, shot to death. Animal or man, whichever — put to death.' A long blast from the horn will signal that it's safe to climb the mountain."

Moses went down the mountain to the people and prepared them for the holy meeting. They gave their clothes a good scrubbing. Then he addressed the people: "Be ready in three days. Don't sleep with a woman."
On the third day at daybreak, there were loud claps of thunder, flashes of lightning, a thick cloud covering the mountain, and an ear-piercing trumpet blast. Everyone in the camp trembled in fear.
Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God. They stood at attention at the base of the mountain.

Mount Sinai was all smoke because God had come down on it as fire. Smoke poured from it like smoke from a furnace. The whole mountain shook and heaved. The trumpet blasts grew louder and louder. Moses spoke, and God answered in thunder. God descended to the peak of Mount Sinai. God called Moses up to the peak, and Moses climbed up.

God said to Moses, "Go down. Warn the people not to break through the barricades to get a look at God, or many of them will die. And warn the priests too — tell them to prepare themselves for the holy meeting, or God will break out against them."
Moses said to God, "But the people can't climb Mount Sinai. You've already warned us well, telling us: 'Post boundaries around the mountain. Respect the holy mountain.'"
God told him, "Go down, then bring Aaron back up with you. But make sure the priests and the people don't break through and come up to God, or he'll break out against them."
So Moses went down to the people. He told them:

paragraphs: God spoke all these words: I am God, your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of a life of slavery.
No other gods, only me.

No carved gods of any size, shape, or form of anything whatever — whether of things that fly or walk or swim. Don't bow down to them and don't serve them, because I am God, your God, and I'm a most jealous God, punishing the children for any sins their parents pass on to them — to the third, and yes, even to the fourth generation of those who hate me. But I'm unswervingly loyal to the thousands who love me and keep my commandments.
No using the name of God, your God, in curses or silly banter; God won't put up with the irreverent use of his name.

Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Work six days and do everything you need to do. But the seventh day is a Sabbath to God, your God. Don't do any work — not you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your servant, nor your maid, nor your animals, not even the foreign guest visiting in your town. For in six days God made heaven, earth, and sea, and everything in them; he rested on the seventh day. Therefore God blessed the Sabbath day; he set it apart as a holy day.
Honor your father and mother so that you'll live a long time in the land that God, your God, is giving you.
No murder.
No adultery.
No stealing.
No lies about your neighbor.
No lusting after your neighbor's house — or wife or servant or maid or ox or donkey. Don't set your heart on anything that is your neighbor's.

All the people, experiencing the thunder and lightning, the trumpet blast and the smoking mountain, were afraid — they pulled back and stood at a distance. They said to Moses, "You speak to us and we'll listen, but don't have God speak to us or we'll die."

The people kept their distance while Moses approached the thick cloud where God was.

paragraphs: "These are the laws you are to place before them:"

"When you buy a Hebrew slave, he will serve six years. In the seventh year he goes free, for nothing. If he came in single, he leaves single. If he came in married, he leaves with his wife. If the master gives him a wife and she gives him sons and daughters, the wife and children stay with the master and he leaves by himself. But suppose the slave says, 'I love my master and my wife and children — I don't want my freedom,' then his master is to bring him before God and to a door or doorpost and pierce his ear with an awl — a sign that he is a slave for life."

"When a man sells his daughter to be a handmaid, she doesn't go free after six years like the men. If she doesn't please her master, her family must buy her back; her master doesn't have the right to sell her to foreigners, since he broke his word to her. If he gives her to his son, he has to treat her like a daughter. If he marries another woman, she keeps all her full rights to meals, clothing, and marital relations. If he won't do any of these three things for her, she goes free, for nothing."

"If someone hits another and death results, the penalty is death. But if there was no intent to kill — if it was an accident, an 'act of God' — I'll set aside a place where the killer can flee for refuge. But if the murder was premeditated, cunningly plotted, then drag the killer away — even from my Altar — to be put to death."
"If someone hits his father or mother, the penalty is death."
"If someone kidnaps a person, the penalty is death — whether the person has been sold or is still being held."
"If someone curses his father or mother, the penalty is death."

"If a quarrel breaks out and one hits the other with a rock or a fist, and the injured one doesn't die but is confined to bed, and then later gets better and can get around on a crutch — the one who hit him is in the clear, except he must pay for the lost time and make sure of complete recovery."

"If a slave owner hits a slave, male or female, with a stick and the slave dies on the spot, the slave must be avenged. But if the slave survives a day or two, he's not to be avenged — the slave is the owner's property."

"When there's a fight and in the fight a pregnant woman is hit so that she miscarries but is not otherwise hurt, the one responsible has to pay whatever the husband demands in compensation. But if there is further damage, then you must give life for life — eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise."

"If a slave owner hits the eye of a slave or handmaid and ruins it, the owner must let the slave go free because of the eye. If the owner knocks out the tooth of the male or female slave, the slave must be released and go free because of the tooth."

"If an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox must be stoned. The meat cannot be eaten, but the owner of the ox is in the clear. But if the ox has a history of goring and the owner knew it and did nothing to guard against it, then if the ox kills a man or a woman, the ox is to be stoned and the owner given the death penalty. If a ransom is agreed upon instead of death, he must pay it in full as a redemption for his life. If a son or daughter is gored, the same judgment holds. If it is a slave or a handmaid the ox gores, thirty shekels of silver is to be paid to the owner and the ox stoned."

"If someone uncovers a cistern or digs a pit and leaves it open, and an ox or donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit must pay whatever the animal is worth to its owner but can keep the dead animal."

"If someone's ox injures a neighbor's ox and the ox dies, they must sell the live ox and split the price; they must also split the dead animal. But if the ox had a history of goring and the owner knew it and did nothing to guard against it, the owner must pay an ox for an ox but can keep the dead animal."
title: The Laws

paragraphs: "If someone steals an ox or a lamb and slaughters or sells it, the thief must pay five cattle in place of the ox and four sheep in place of the lamb. If the thief is caught while breaking in and is hit hard and dies, there is no bloodguilt. But if it happens after daybreak, there is bloodguilt."

"A thief must make full restitution for what is stolen. The thief who can't pay is to be sold for his thieving. If he's caught red-handed with the stolen goods, and the ox or donkey or lamb is still alive, the thief pays double."
"If someone grazes livestock in a field or vineyard but lets them loose so they graze in someone else's field, restitution must be made from the best of the owner's field or vineyard."
"If fire breaks out and spreads to the brush so that the sheaves of grain or the standing grain or even the whole field is burned up, whoever started the fire must pay for the damages."

"If someone gives a neighbor money or things for safekeeping and they're stolen from the neighbor's house — the thief, if caught, must pay back double. If the thief isn't caught, the owner must be brought before God to determine whether the owner was the one who took the neighbor's goods."

"In all cases of stolen goods — oxen, donkeys, sheep, clothing, anything at all missing of which someone says, 'That's mine' — both parties must come before the judges. The one the judges pronounce guilty must pay double to the other."

"If someone gives a donkey or ox or lamb or any kind of animal to another for safekeeping and it dies or is injured or lost and there's no witness, an oath before God must be made between them to decide whether one has laid hands on the other's property. The owner must accept this and no damages are assessed. But if it turns out it was stolen, the owner must be compensated. If it's been torn by wild beasts, the torn animal must be brought in as evidence; no damages have to be paid."

"If someone borrows an animal from a neighbor and it gets injured or dies while the owner isn't present, he must pay for it. But if the owner was with it, he doesn't have to pay. If the animal was hired, the payment covers the loss."

"If a man seduces a virgin who isn't engaged to be married and sleeps with her, he must pay the marriage price and marry her. If her father absolutely refuses to give her away, the man must still pay the marriage price for virgins."
"Don't let a sorceress live."
"Anyone who has sex with an animal gets the death penalty."
"Anyone who sacrifices to a god other than God alone must be put to death."
"Don't abuse or take advantage of strangers; remember, you were once strangers in Egypt."

"Don't mistreat widows or orphans. If you do and they cry out to me, you can be sure I'll take them most seriously; I'll show my anger and come raging among you with the sword, and your wives will end up widows and your children orphans."
"If you lend money to my people — to any of the down-and-out among you — don't come down hard on them and gouge them with interest."

"If you take your neighbor's coat as security, give it back before nightfall; it may be your neighbor's only covering — what else does the person have to sleep in? And if I hear the neighbor crying out from the cold, I'll step in — I'm compassionate."
"Don't curse God; and don't damn your leaders."
"Don't be stingy as your wine vats fill up. Dedicate your firstborn sons to me. The same with your cattle and sheep — they're to stay seven days with their mother, then give them to me."
"Be holy for my sake. Don't eat mutilated flesh you find in the fields; throw it to the dogs."

paragraphs: "Don't pass on malicious gossip. Don't link up with a wicked person and give corrupt testimony. Don't go along with the crowd in doing evil, and don't mess up your testimony in a case just to please the crowd. And just because someone is poor, don't show favoritism in a dispute."
"If you find your enemy's ox or donkey loose, take it back to him. If you see the donkey of someone who hates you lying helpless under its load, don't walk off and leave it. Help it up."
"When there's a dispute concerning your poor, don't tamper with the justice due them."
"Stay clear of false accusations. Don't contribute to the death of innocent and good people. I don't let the wicked off the hook."
"Don't take bribes. Bribes blind perfectly good eyes and twist the speech of good people."
"Don't take advantage of a stranger. You know what it's like to be a stranger; you were strangers in Egypt."

"Sow your land for six years and gather in its crops, but in the seventh year leave it alone and give it a rest so that your poor may eat from it. What they leave, let the wildlife have. Do the same with your vineyards and olive groves."
"Work for six days and rest the seventh, so your ox and donkey may rest and your servant and migrant workers may have time to get their needed rest."
"Listen carefully to everything I tell you. Don't pay attention to other gods — don't so much as mention their names."
"Three times a year you are to hold a festival for me."

"Hold the spring Festival of Unraised Bread when you eat unraised bread for seven days at the time set for the month of Abib, as I commanded you. That was the month you came out of Egypt. No one should show up before me empty-handed."

"Hold the summer Festival of Harvest when you bring in the firstfruits of all your work in the fields. Hold the autumn Festival of Ingathering at the end of the season when you bring in the year's crops."
"Three times a year all your males are to appear before the Master, God."
"Don't offer the blood of a sacrifice to me with anything that has yeast in it. Don't leave the fat from my festival offering out overnight."
"Bring the choice first produce of the year to the house of your God. Don't boil a kid in its mother's milk."

"Now get yourselves ready. I'm sending my Angel ahead of you to guard you in your travels, to lead you to the place that I've prepared. Pay close attention to him. Obey him. Don't go against him. He won't put up with your rebellions because he's acting on my authority. But if you obey him and do everything I tell you, I'll be an enemy to your enemies, I'll fight those who fight you. When my Angel goes ahead of you and leads you to the land of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, I'll clear the country of them. So don't worship or serve their gods; don't do anything they do, because I'm going to wipe them right off the face of the earth and smash their sacred phallic pillars to bits."

"But you — you serve your God and he'll bless your food and your water. I'll get rid of the sickness among you; there won't be any miscarriages nor barren women in your land. I'll make sure you live full and complete lives."
"I'll send my Terror on ahead of you and throw those peoples you're approaching into a panic. All you'll see of your enemies is the backs of their necks."

"And I'll send Despair on ahead of you. It will push the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites out of your way. I won't get rid of them all at once, or the land will grow up in weeds and the wild animals will take over. Little by little I'll get them out of there while you have a chance to get your crops going and make the land your own. I will make your borders stretch from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean Sea and from the Wilderness to the Euphrates River. I'm turning everyone living in that land over to you; go ahead and drive them out."
"Don't make any deals with them or their gods. They are not to stay in the same country with you, or they'll get you to sin by worshiping their gods. Beware. That's a huge danger."
title: Justice and Festivals
